speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I understand you are experiencing dizziness, nausea, and imbalance; to help me determine the cause, could you please describe when these symptoms first started and if they are constant or intermittent?

speaker: Patient
text: 27-year-old male. The patient reports a sustained sensation of the room spinning since this morning, which is low grade and constant. He occasionally feels nauseous and has taken diphenhydramine to help him sleep, which also alleviates his symptoms slightly. He mentions recent increased intake of garlic due to trying to recover from a cold a few days ago. Past medical history is unremarkable.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Vestibular Neuritis.

The patient's description of a constant, low-grade spinning sensation starting this morning, along with nausea and relief from diphenhydramine, is classic for vestibular neuritis. The recent garlic intake and history of a cold suggest a viral etiology, but the lack of hearing loss helps rule out labyrinthitis. Since the symptoms are constant rather than episodic, this makes benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) less likely. I will proceed with this diagnosis based on the clinical presentation.
